name: llama.cpp
one_liner: The C/C++ engine that runs GGUF models on almost any computer. Many apps on this list use it underneath.
strengths: It runs on CUDA, ROCm, Vulkan, Metal, SYCL and plain CPU, and it can split a model between GPU and system RAM. New model types usually arrive here first, and the built-in server has a chat page plus OpenAI- and Anthropic-style APIs.
limits: You control it with command-line flags, which takes some learning. It serves many users at once less efficiently than vLLM or SGLang on big GPUs.
commercial_note: MIT licence, fine for business use. The model you load has its own licence.
last_checked_state: active; build b12536 released 2026-11-19; v1.0.0 version scheme announced 2026-11-13; ggml.ai team joined Hugging Face 2026-02-20

name: Llama (llama.app desktop app)
one_liner: A small official app from the llama.cpp team that downloads and runs models from the menu bar (Mac) or system tray (Windows).
strengths: It suggests models that fit your machine and shows a memory estimate for each context length. It runs a standard llama.cpp server, so other apps can connect to it.
limits: It is new and has fewer settings than LM Studio or Jan. Linux gets only the command-line tool, and GPU support depends on which llama.cpp build it downloads.
commercial_note: MIT licence (Hugging Face / llama.cpp team). The Windows README says it sends no telemetry.
last_checked_state: active; macOS app 0.48.0 released 2026-11-17; Windows app v0.14.1 released 2026-10-30

name: Ollama
one_liner: A background service plus a simple app that downloads and runs models with one command such as 'ollama run'.
strengths: Installing and running a model takes two commands, and many other tools connect to Ollama directly. It picks GPU and memory settings for you and unloads models when they are idle.
limits: It hides many settings, so tuning context length or GPU layers is less direct than in llama.cpp. Its model library uses its own names and storage, which other tools cannot read as plain GGUF files without extra steps.
commercial_note: MIT licence. Ollama's cloud models are a separate online service with their own terms; local use does not need an account.

name: LM Studio
one_liner: A polished desktop app to search, download and chat with local models, with a built-in local server.
strengths: It shows which model files fit your hardware before you download them. On Macs it can use MLX as well as llama.cpp, and a headless mode (llmster) runs it on servers.
limits: The app is closed source. Macs need Apple silicon and macOS 14 or newer; Intel Macs are not supported.
commercial_note: Free for home and work since 2025-07-08, no separate licence needed. The app terms (updated 2026-08-23) allow personal and internal business use but forbid redistribution, reverse engineering and offering it as a hosted service. Paid Teams/Enterprise plans exist.
last_checked_state: active; LM Studio 0.4.28 on the download page (checked 2026-11-19); separate agent app LM Studio Bionic 1.2.1 released 2026-11-16

name: Jan
one_liner: An open-source chat app for local models, built on llama.cpp, with an optional local API server.
strengths: It is fully open source and works offline. It ships CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, Metal and CPU builds of llama.cpp and a local server on port 1337.
limits: It has fewer advanced settings and model-fit hints than LM Studio. It is made for one person on one machine.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: llamafile
one_liner: Packs a model and llama.cpp into one file that runs on most operating systems without installing anything.
strengths: You download one file and run it, which suits demos, classrooms and offline machines. It bundles the llama.cpp server and a Whisper-based speech tool.
limits: On Windows a single executable must be under 4 GB, so larger models need a separate GGUF file. The 0.10 rebuild may lack some features of the older 0.9 releases.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0; its changes to llama.cpp and whisper.cpp are MIT. Maintained by Mozilla.ai.

name: KoboldCpp
one_liner: A single-file app that runs GGUF text models and also does images, speech-to-text and text-to-speech.
strengths: One download gives you text, image (via stable-diffusion.cpp), Whisper and TTS in one place. It offers KoboldAI, OpenAI, Ollama and A1111-style APIs, so many front ends can use it.
limits: The interface is aimed at chat, role-play and story writing, which can feel busy. Mac users with Intel chips must build it from source, and ROCm needs a manual build or a community fork.
commercial_note: AGPL-3.0: if you change the code and offer it to others over a network, you must share your changes. Using it unmodified inside a company is fine.

name: textgen (formerly text-generation-webui)
one_liner: A browser-based chat app that can switch between several engines: llama.cpp, ExLlamaV3, Transformers and TensorRT-LLM.
strengths: It lets you try different engines and model formats from one interface. Portable builds for CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm and CPU need no install.
limits: There are many settings, which can confuse beginners. Releases slowed in 2026; the last tagged release was in May.
commercial_note: AGPL-3.0: share your changes if you offer a modified version over a network.
last_checked_state: slowing; repo renamed to oobabooga/textgen; v4.9 released 2026-05-20; last commit 2026-08-17

name: Open WebUI
one_liner: A self-hosted ChatGPT-style web interface that connects to Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible server. It does not run models itself.
license: Open WebUI License (BSD-3 based, with branding clause)
strengths: It adds user accounts, chat history, document upload and tools on top of your model server. It works with local servers and cloud APIs at the same time.
limits: Speed depends entirely on the model server behind it. It is a large application, and updates sometimes need care with your data.
commercial_note: Since v0.6.6 (April 2025) you may not remove or change the Open WebUI branding, unless you have 50 or fewer users in any 30-day period or buy an enterprise licence. The project says this licence is not OSI-approved open source. Code up to v0.6.5 stays BSD-3.

name: MLX / mlx-lm
one_liner: Apple's machine-learning framework for Apple silicon, plus a Python package that runs and fine-tunes LLMs with it.
strengths: It uses the Mac's unified memory well and is often faster than llama.cpp on Apple silicon. It can quantise models and do LoRA fine-tuning on a Mac.
limits: It runs only on Apple silicon Macs. Its HTTP server is basic and its own docs say it is not for production.
commercial_note: MIT licence. LM Studio and Ollama use MLX on Macs, so you may not need to install it yourself.
last_checked_state: active; mlx-lm v0.32.2 released 2026-10-16; MLX v0.32.4 released 2026-10-14

name: vLLM
one_liner: A high-throughput server engine for serving models to many users at once on data-centre or workstation GPUs.
strengths: PagedAttention and continuous batching let one GPU serve many requests at once. It supports most new models quickly and scales across several GPUs and machines.
limits: It reserves most of the GPU memory at start-up and expects the whole model to fit in VRAM. The docs list no native Windows build, and Apple GPUs need a separate vLLM-Metal plugin.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: SGLang
one_liner: A fast serving engine for LLMs and multimodal models, similar in purpose to vLLM.
strengths: RadixAttention reuses shared prompt prefixes, which helps chat and agent workloads. It also runs on Intel Xeon CPUs, Google TPUs and Ascend NPUs, and has a diffusion add-on for images and video.
limits: Like vLLM it reserves a fixed share of VRAM and is built for servers, not laptops. Setup and tuning assume Linux and some ops experience.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: TensorRT-LLM
one_liner: NVIDIA's own library for the fastest LLM serving on NVIDIA data-centre and RTX GPUs.
strengths: It has hand-tuned kernels for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, including FP8 and NVFP4. 'trtllm-serve' starts an OpenAI-compatible server.
limits: It works only on NVIDIA GPUs, and Windows support was deprecated in v0.18. Most recent GitHub releases are release candidates, and anonymous telemetry is on by default.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0. Turn off telemetry if your company requires it (the README lists opt-out methods).
last_checked_state: active; v1.4.0rc4 pre-release 2026-11-18; latest stable on PyPI 1.2.1 (2026-04-20); the old TensorRT engine backend was removed, PyTorch backend only

name: Hugging Face TGI (Text Generation Inference)
one_liner: ARCHIVED. Hugging Face's former production LLM server. New projects should use vLLM, SGLang or llama.cpp.
strengths: Existing Docker deployments keep working. It had an OpenAI-compatible Messages API.
limits: The repository is read-only and gets no fixes. Its README recommends vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp or MLX instead.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, but unmaintained software is a security risk for business use.
last_checked_state: archived 2026-03-21 after a maintenance-mode period; last release v3.3.7 on 2025-12-19

name: LMDeploy
one_liner: A serving and quantisation toolkit from the InternLM team, an alternative to vLLM.
strengths: Its TurboMind engine is fast for 4-bit AWQ models and supports int8/int4 KV-cache quantisation. It also supports Huawei Ascend through its PyTorch engine.
limits: Model support is narrower than vLLM's and differs between its two engines. Documentation and community are smaller outside China.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: NVIDIA Dynamo
one_liner: A layer that coordinates vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM across many GPUs and machines in a data centre.
strengths: It routes requests to GPUs that already hold the right cache and can split prompt processing and generation onto different GPUs. It suits large clusters run on Kubernetes.
limits: Its own README says a single model on a single GPU probably does not need it. It adds a lot of moving parts.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0. The engines underneath keep their own licences.

name: NVIDIA NIM
one_liner: Ready-made NVIDIA containers that serve a specific model with an OpenAI-compatible API.
strengths: NVIDIA picks and tests the engine settings for each model and GPU. Recent versions use vLLM and SGLang inside.
limits: It needs an NVIDIA account and NVIDIA GPUs, and you can only run models NVIDIA has packaged. Containers are large.
commercial_note: Free for development, testing and research for NVIDIA Developer Program members (up to 16 GPUs). Serving real users counts as production and needs an NVIDIA AI Enterprise licence (90-day free trial available).
last_checked_state: active; NIM for LLMs 3.0.0 listed in NVIDIA docs (release date not verified)

name: LocalAI
one_liner: A self-hosted server that copies the OpenAI API for text, images, speech and more, using many backends.
strengths: One server covers chat, embeddings, images, speech-to-text and text-to-speech. It detects your GPU and downloads a matching backend (llama.cpp, vLLM, whisper.cpp and others).
limits: With over 80 backends, problems can be hard to trace. Windows is not listed; use Docker there.
commercial_note: Code is MIT. The LocalAI name and logo are reserved, so do not use them for your own product.

name: Docker Model Runner
one_liner: Docker's built-in way to pull models like container images and run them with llama.cpp, vLLM or Diffusers.
strengths: Teams already using Docker can store and share models in the same registries as their containers. It offers OpenAI- and Ollama-compatible APIs.
limits: vLLM and Diffusers modes need NVIDIA GPUs (Linux, or Windows with WSL2 for vLLM). The API has no authentication, so do not expose it to a network.
commercial_note: Model Runner code is Apache-2.0. Docker Desktop itself needs a paid subscription at companies with 250+ employees or more than $10M revenue; Docker Engine on Linux does not.

name: ExLlamaV3 + TabbyAPI
one_liner: A fast engine for NVIDIA consumer GPUs with its own EXL3 quantisation format; TabbyAPI is its API server.
strengths: EXL3 keeps good quality at low bit rates, so bigger models fit on one gaming GPU. It supports tensor-parallel across several consumer GPUs and offloading MoE experts to the CPU.
limits: It is documented for NVIDIA GPUs only. TabbyAPI is a hobby project and its author says it is not meant for production servers.
commercial_note: ExLlamaV3 is MIT. TabbyAPI is AGPL-3.0: share changes if you offer a modified version over a network.
last_checked_state: active; ExLlamaV3 1.6.7 released 2026-11-14; TabbyAPI has no tagged releases (rolling), last commit 2026-11-14

name: llama-swap
one_liner: A small proxy that starts and stops model servers on demand, so one API address can offer many models.
strengths: It reads the model name in each request and launches the matching llama.cpp, vLLM or other server. One Go binary and a YAML file are all you need, and a web page shows logs and lets you load or unload models.
limits: It does no inference itself, so you still set up each server. Switching models takes time because the old one is stopped first.
commercial_note: MIT, fine for business use.

name: Lemonade
one_liner: An AMD-sponsored local AI server and app that runs models on Radeon GPUs, Ryzen AI NPUs and other hardware.
strengths: It is the easiest way to use the NPU in Ryzen AI laptops and the large shared memory of Ryzen AI Max (Strix Halo) systems. It bundles llama.cpp (Vulkan/ROCm), whisper.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp behind OpenAI, Anthropic and Ollama-style APIs.
limits: NPU models must be specially prepared, so the NPU model list is smaller. Its main focus is AMD hardware.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: OpenVINO GenAI
one_liner: Intel's library for running LLMs, image and speech models on Intel CPUs, GPUs and NPUs.
strengths: It gets good speed from Intel Core Ultra iGPUs and NPUs and from Arc graphics cards. Many models are ready-converted in the OpenVINO organisation on Hugging Face.
limits: You usually need to convert models to OpenVINO format first. It is a Python/C++ library, so you write a little code or use the Model Server.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: OpenVINO Model Server (OVMS)
one_liner: Intel's server that exposes OpenVINO models through OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
strengths: It covers chat, embeddings, image generation and speech with continuous batching. It runs on Xeon servers as well as Intel client PCs, in Docker or as a Windows binary.
limits: It is tuned for Intel hardware and gives little benefit on NVIDIA or AMD GPUs. Setup takes more steps than desktop apps.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: IPEX-LLM
one_liner: ARCHIVED. Intel's former library for running LLMs on Intel GPUs. Use OpenVINO, llama.cpp (SYCL or Vulkan) or vLLM on Intel XPU instead.
strengths: Old guides and portable builds still exist. It once offered Intel-GPU builds of Ollama and llama.cpp.
limits: The repository is read-only and Intel says it will not develop or support it. GitHub flags it as having known security issues.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0, but archived software with known security issues should not be used in business settings.

name: ONNX Runtime GenAI
one_liner: Microsoft's library that runs LLMs in ONNX format on CPUs, GPUs and NPUs, mainly for developers building apps.
strengths: It has APIs for Python, C#, C++ and Java, so it fits into desktop and mobile apps. On Windows it can use DirectML to reach most GPUs.
limits: Models must be converted to ONNX first, and fewer models are available ready-made. Its docs still label the generate() API as preview.
commercial_note: MIT, fine for business use.
last_checked_state: active; 0.20.0 on PyPI 2026-11-14 (GitHub repo page returned 404 when checked 2026-11-19)

name: Foundry Local
one_liner: Microsoft's on-device AI runtime and SDK that ships a curated set of optimised models inside your app.
license: MIT (SDK); runtime under Microsoft product terms
strengths: It picks the best GPU, NPU or CPU path automatically and adds about 20 MB to an app. It has SDKs for C#, C++, JavaScript, Rust and Python and an optional OpenAI-compatible local server.
limits: You can only use models from Microsoft's curated catalogue. Microsoft says it is for one user per device, not for serving many users.
commercial_note: SDK is MIT. The runtime and each model are governed by Microsoft's product terms and the model licences. No Azure subscription needed.
last_checked_state: active; GA since 2026-04-09; Python SDK 2.5.0 on PyPI 2026-11-17 (GitHub repo page returned 404 when checked)

name: ComfyUI
one_liner: A node-based app for generating images, video, audio and 3D with open models, where you connect boxes into a workflow.
strengths: New image and video models usually work here first, and shared workflow files make results repeatable. Its memory manager streams weights so large models can run on small GPUs.
limits: The node graph looks complex at first. Community custom nodes run arbitrary code, so install only ones you trust.
commercial_note: GPL-3.0 covers the software; images you make are not affected. Optional paid 'partner nodes' call online services and can be switched off with --disable-partner-nodes. Model licences vary (some are non-commercial).
last_checked_state: active; v0.46.0 released 2026-11-18 (repo now under Comfy-Org)

name: Hugging Face Diffusers
one_liner: A Python library for running and training image, video and audio diffusion models.
strengths: Most new diffusion models publish official Diffusers support on day one. Offloading and quantisation options help large models run on smaller GPUs.
limits: You write Python code; there is no app. Speed and memory use depend on which optimisations you turn on.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0. Each model has its own licence.

name: stable-diffusion.cpp
one_liner: A C/C++ engine for image and video diffusion models, built on the same ggml library as llama.cpp.
strengths: It needs no Python and runs on CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, SYCL, OpenCL or CPU. It supports SD, SDXL, FLUX, Qwen Image, Wan and LTX video, and quantised GGUF weights.
limits: It is mostly a command-line tool; the built-in web page in sd-server is simple. It has fewer extras such as ControlNet workflows than ComfyUI.
commercial_note: MIT. KoboldCpp and Lemonade use it inside. Model licences vary.

name: InvokeAI
one_liner: A polished image-generation app with a canvas for painting, inpainting and layers.
strengths: The launcher installs everything, and the canvas suits people who think like artists. It supports SD1.5, SDXL, SD 3.5, FLUX variants, Qwen Image, Z-Image and others.
limits: It adds new model types more slowly than ComfyUI. Local video generation is not in its model list.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0. The Invoke company team joined Adobe in October 2025 and the hosted service closed; the open-source project is now community-run.
last_checked_state: active (community-maintained); v6.14.4 released 2026-11-03; v7.0.0 beta 1 on 2026-11-09

name: Forge Neo / Forge Classic (Stable Diffusion WebUI Forge fork)
one_liner: A maintained fork of the Forge web UI, the classic tab-based image generator descended from AUTOMATIC1111.
strengths: The familiar A1111-style layout works with most old tutorials and extensions. The Neo branch adds FLUX, Qwen Image, Z-Image and Wan 2.2.
limits: It is mainly tested on NVIDIA; the maintainer says AMD issues will be ignored. The original lllyasviel Forge and AUTOMATIC1111 repositories have had little or no development since 2025.
commercial_note: AGPL-3.0: share your changes if you offer a modified version over a network. Model licences vary.
last_checked_state: active; fork release 2.32 on 2026-11-10. Original lllyasviel/stable-diffusion-webui-forge: no commits since 2025-07-31

name: Fooocus
one_liner: MAINTENANCE ONLY. A very simple SDXL image generator where you mostly just type a prompt.
strengths: It hides almost all settings and gives good SDXL results quickly. It still works for SDXL models.
limits: It gets bug fixes only and will not add newer models such as FLUX. Its README points to Forge, ComfyUI or SwarmUI for newer models.
commercial_note: GPL-3.0. SDXL model licences apply to the models.
last_checked_state: limited long-term support (bug fixes only); last release v2.5.5 on 2024-08-12; last commit 2025-12-01

name: SD.Next
one_liner: An all-in-one web UI for image and video generation that supports a very wide range of hardware.
strengths: It supports ROCm and ZLUDA on AMD, IPEX on Intel Arc, OpenVINO, Apple MPS and CPU. It is updated often with new models.
limits: The many options can overwhelm beginners. Frequent updates sometimes change settings.
commercial_note: Apache-2.0. Model licences vary.

name: WanGP (Wan2GP)
one_liner: A web app for video (and image, audio) generation tuned to run on GPUs with little VRAM.
strengths: The project says some models run on 4 GB of VRAM and 8 GB is enough to start. It bundles Wan, LTX, Hunyuan Video and image models with a queue and headless mode.
limits: Low-VRAM tricks make generation slow, and the VRAM figures are the project's own claims. Apple GPUs are not mentioned.
commercial_note: Free to use, including at work, and you may sell outputs (credit WanGP). You may not resell it, white-label it or offer it as a paid hosted service without a separate licence. Model licences apply separately.
last_checked_state: active; repo renamed to WanGP; last commit 2026-11-17; latest GitHub release WanGP Manager 0.1.18 (2026-11-17)

name: whisper.cpp
one_liner: A C/C++ version of OpenAI's Whisper speech-to-text model that runs on almost any device.
strengths: It is fast on Apple silicon (Metal and Core ML) and runs well on plain CPUs. It supports CUDA, Vulkan, OpenVINO, ROCm and quantised models.
limits: Its server has an 'OAI-like' API that is not fully OpenAI-compatible. It does not identify speakers.
commercial_note: MIT. Whisper model weights are MIT too.

name: faster-whisper
one_liner: A Python reimplementation of Whisper on the CTranslate2 engine, up to 4x faster than the original.
strengths: int8 mode cuts memory use, and the batched pipeline transcribes long files much faster on a GPU. WhisperX and speaches build on it.
limits: GPU acceleration is NVIDIA only. It is a library with no server; releases have slowed.
commercial_note: MIT, fine for business use.

name: WhisperX
one_liner: Whisper transcription with word-level timestamps and speaker labels (who spoke when).
strengths: It adds precise word timings and speaker diarisation on top of faster-whisper. Good for meeting notes and subtitles.
limits: Speaker diarisation uses pyannote models that need a Hugging Face account and accepting their terms. It is a command-line tool and library, not an app.
commercial_note: BSD-2-Clause. Check the pyannote model terms for business use.

name: speaches
one_liner: An OpenAI-compatible server for speech-to-text and text-to-speech, using faster-whisper, Kokoro and Piper.
strengths: Apps written for OpenAI's audio API can use it unchanged. It loads models on request and unloads them when idle, including a Realtime API.
limits: It is run through Docker and is still at pre-release versions. Some features in its README are marked TODO.
commercial_note: MIT. Voice and model licences vary.
last_checked_state: active development; latest tag v0.9.0-rc.3 (2025-12-27); last commit 2026-11-19

name: Kokoro-FastAPI
one_liner: A Docker server for the small Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model with an OpenAI-compatible speech endpoint.
strengths: Kokoro is small enough to run fast on a CPU and sounds natural. The server offers /v1/audio/speech, streaming and a simple web player.
limits: It has a fixed set of voices and does not clone voices. AMD support is experimental and Apple runs without Docker.
commercial_note: Wrapper and Kokoro-82M weights are both Apache-2.0, fine for business use.

name: Coqui TTS (Idiap fork, coqui-tts)
one_liner: The community-maintained continuation of Coqui TTS, a toolkit with many text-to-speech models including XTTS.
strengths: It includes many models and languages, plus voice cloning with XTTS v2. It is kept working with new Python and PyTorch versions.
limits: It is a Python toolkit aimed at developers and researchers. Newer TTS models often sound better.
commercial_note: Code is MPL-2.0. The popular XTTS-v2 weights use the Coqui Public Model License, which does not allow commercial use.
last_checked_state: active; v0.28.0 released 2026-10-19 (original coqui-ai company shut down in 2024)

name: Chatterbox (Resemble AI)
one_liner: RETIRED. Open text-to-speech models with voice cloning; the code stays online but is no longer maintained.
strengths: It clones a voice from about 10 seconds of audio and has English, multilingual (23+ languages) and small CPU-friendly variants. It still works as a Python library with Gradio demos.
limits: Its README says it has been retired research since August 2026, with no support or updates. It has no server or API of its own.
commercial_note: MIT. Every output carries an inaudible Perth watermark.
last_checked_state: retired (README: no longer maintained as of August 2026); last PyPI release 0.1.7 on 2026-03-26

name: Piper
one_liner: A small, fast text-to-speech engine that runs well on CPUs and Raspberry Pi, used by Home Assistant.
strengths: It is quick even on weak hardware and has many voices and languages. Install with 'pip install piper-tts'; it has a simple HTTP server.
limits: Voices sound more robotic than larger modern TTS models. The old rhasspy/piper repository is archived, so use the new OHF-Voice repository.
commercial_note: The new version is GPL-3.0 (the archived original was MIT). Each voice has its own licence; check before commercial use.
last_checked_state: moved: rhasspy/piper archived (last push 2025-08-26); continues as OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl, v1.8.0 released 2026-09-04
